extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of language, and inductive method
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts principles about names, connotation/denotation, definition, categories, and valid forms of propositions and syllogisms in philosophical logic. Focused on how terms should be used and how definitions and propositions ought to be evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using vague common names without qualification
rubrics_metrics.description: “Such a term is wholly unfit for accurate reasoning, unless hedged round on every occasion by other phrases; as building stone, precious stone, gall-stone, etc.” (example: Stone applied to many disparate things)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a familiar term covers heterogeneous referents (e.g. 'stone' for minerals, fruit kernels, calculi), do not use it for precise reasoning unless qualified by additional phrases specifying which sense is meant. The method of definition will fail if there is insufficient community of usage to ground a single uniform meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test a name's denotation by what it can be predicated of
rubrics_metrics.description: “The test of what a name denotes is what it can be predicated of.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To determine the denotation of a name, ask whether a given predicate can be truthfully ascribed to entities the name is supposed to denote (e.g. one can predicate 'not-white' of a sound or smell). Use predicate-applicability as the practical test of denotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise, consistently-defined technical terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt terms exclusively appropriated to express particular logical ideas (example: use 'to connote' in a precise technical sense to mark attributes involved in signification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When common terms are ambiguous or used differently by authorities (e.g., James Mill), define and use a term consistently for the technical purpose needed to communicate clearly in philosophy/logic. Historical or schoolmen usages can be invoked where they give precise technical senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish connotation and denotation in definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete general names mark attributes (connotation), and their meaning involves both denotation (what they point to) and connotation (the attributes included).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit whether a definition is specifying what a name denotes (extension) or what it connotes (intension/attributes). Failure to distinguish these leads to confusion in analyzing propositions and definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer definitions that reflect common (ordinary) signification unless specifying scientific connotation
rubrics_metrics.description: A name means only the properties which it is a mark of in the general mind; special scientific connotation is apart and must be explicitly stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat as part of a word's ordinary meaning those factual properties known only to specialists; when using terms in a scientific sense, declare that special connotation. This preserves the distinction between verbal and real propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real vs. Verbal Propositions — criterion for information content
rubrics_metrics.description: The division of propositions into real and verbal discriminates propositions that convey information about facts from those which do not; a proposition that affirms an attribute already implicit in the name's common signification adds no information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a proposition asserts anything beyond the common meaning of the terms. If it does not (given ordinary usage), treat it as verbal; if it supplies new factual information, treat it as real and subject to empirical proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition completeness criterion (Bain's view) — 'sum of all properties connoted by the name'
rubrics_metrics.description: Bain: 'the definition in its full import, is the sum of all the properties connoted by the name; it exhausts the meaning of a word.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One approach to definition requires enumerating ultimate, underivable properties that attach to a term (scientific/technical viewpoint). Poincaré critiques extending this to ordinary usage; decide whether the task is exhaustive scientific definition or ordinary nominal definition before judging adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient-definition-for-distinction (De Morgan's view)
rubrics_metrics.description: De Morgan: a 'real' definition may contain less than the nominal definition provided it is sufficient to separate the things contained under that word from all others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the purpose is identification or classification rather than exhaustive account, a definition adequate for distinction (even if partial) is acceptable. Use concise distinguishing features when full connotation-enumeration is unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: When converting or analyzing propositions, preserve the modal/ontological status of predicates
rubrics_metrics.description: In syllogisms involving imaginary or modal creatures (e.g., dragons), predicates must carry the same modal/ontological qualification (imagined vs real) to produce valid conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a premise predicates properties of imagined entities, the conclusion must preserve that imagined status (e.g., 'Some serpents either do or are imagined to breathe flame'). Avoid silently shifting from 'imagined' to 'real' in premises or conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Categories as generalizations of predicates (predicate-analysis approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's Categories were conceived as an analysis of the final import of predication (not strictly a classification of all namable things): ask 'Under what Categories can we predicate regarding X?' rather than 'In what Category is X placed?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying categorical schemes, focus on what can be predicated about an item (substance, quantity, quality, relation, etc.) rather than forcing every item into a classificatory pigeonhole. This helps avoid misplaced demands (e.g., absence of a Category of Feeling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious imputing fallacy to arguments based on ambiguous terms without subject knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Many leading terms are used in numerous shades of meaning; a critic may mistake a valid argument for a fallacy by pausing at the apparent double meaning of a term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before declaring an argument fallacious due to ambiguity, ensure sufficient knowledge of the subject matter and search for unobvious links or legitimate senses that the arguer may be employing. Value substantive connections over mere lexical quibbles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize common equivalent propositional transformations (equipollency, obversion, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equivalent propositional forms (e.g., changing an affirmation to denying its negative — obversion) are common and have established rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing or reformulating propositions, be aware of recognized equivalences (obversion, contraposition, etc.) and use them correctly to preserve logical content during transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish extension (subject construed by extension) from intension (predicate construed by intension) but note extension is apprehended through attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Though we naturally construe the subject of a proposition in its extension and the predicate in its intension, the extension (the class denoted) is apprehended solely through the attributes (intension).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In analyzing propositions, remember that perceived scope (extension) is mediated by attributes; do not treat extension and intension as wholly independent in the 'living processes of thought and language.' Use attribute-analysis to clarify extensional claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of Existence as a predicable distinct from Causation or Co-existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Countering Bain: Existence can be predicated apart from causation and co-existence; the abstract name 'Existence' and the concrete name 'Being' have meaning in terms of capacity to excite sensations or states of consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When handling propositions about existence, avoid collapsing 'Existence' into merely elliptical forms of co-existence or causation. Treat existence-claims as having distinct logical status and consider whether the formulation is masking more complex claims about cause or co-presence.
